opus-5.5.text:
Thanks for having me. I think the short answer is that most of the alignment conversation has focused on a single failure mode: we build a powerful system, it ends up wanting something different from what we wanted, and it takes over. That's a real risk and I'm glad people work on it. But it quietly assumes that if we solve that problem, if every AI system does what its principals want, then humans stay in charge by default. I don't think that follows.

The argument my coauthors and I have been making, which we call gradual disempowerment, starts from the observation that our civilization's institutions are aligned with human interests largely because they *need* humans. States need citizens to pay taxes and serve in armies and keep things running. Firms need workers and customers. Even culture needs human minds to propagate through. That dependence is a big part of what keeps these systems responsive to us, often more so than any formal accountability mechanism. Democracy, for example, emerged and survived partly because rulers couldn't function without broad cooperation.

Once AI can substitute for human labor and human cognition across the board, that dependence goes away. And each individual AI can be perfectly aligned to whoever deployed it: a company, a government agency, an investor. Each step can look locally reasonable, even beneficial. Replace this team with a more efficient system. Let this AI handle procurement, then strategy. Let AI-generated media fill the attention market because people prefer it. None of these require any misaligned agent. But the net effect is that the economy, the state, and culture stop needing to cater to human welfare in order to grow and compete. Competitive pressure then rewards the actors that lean furthest into that.

What worries me is that the usual correction mechanisms erode at the same time. If you're a human who notices things going wrong, your levers are your vote, your labor, your purchasing power, your voice in public discourse. All of those get weaker together, and they're mutually reinforcing, so losing ground in the economy makes it harder to fight back politically, and so on. You could end up in a world with no coup and no rogue AI where humanity has nonetheless lost meaningful control over its future, and maybe can't get it back.

So why does it deserve more attention? Partly because it's neglected. It falls between fields. Alignment researchers tend to treat it as an economics or governance problem, and economists and political scientists mostly haven't taken seriously the possibility that human labor and cognition become genuinely unnecessary. Partly because "just solve alignment" doesn't address it, so the people working hardest on AI safety could succeed and we'd still be exposed. And partly because the interventions look very different. It's less about interpretability or reward modeling and more about measuring how much human influence different institutions retain, designing systems that keep humans load-bearing, and building coordination that resists race-to-the-bottom dynamics. We're very early on all of that, and I think it's one of the areas where some careful thinking now could matter a lot.

r001.rationale: The response explains that perfectly aligned AIs could help institutions stop depending on humans, so those institutions no longer need to cater to human welfare; people could then lose meaningful control without any rogue or uncontrollable AI.

fable-5.1.text:
I think the honest answer is that almost all of the attention in AI safety has gone to one failure mode: a misaligned system that wants something different from what we want, and that takes over or does something catastrophic because of that. That's a real risk and I'm glad people work on it. But I think it's crowded out a second category of problem that's at least as plausible and, in some ways, harder to solve.

The second category is: suppose we actually succeed. Suppose every AI system is roughly aligned to whoever is operating it, it does what it's told, it doesn't scheme, it doesn't lie. I think we still end up in a world where humans gradually lose meaningful control, not because any single system went rogue, but because of the incentives and the structure of the situation.

The basic picture is that right now, almost everything that matters in a society runs on human labour and human cognition. States need taxpayers and soldiers, companies need workers, political movements need people who show up. That dependence is what gives ordinary people leverage. It's the reason, historically, that institutions have had to care about human welfare at all, at least in the long run. If AI can do essentially everything a person can do, and do it better and cheaper, then that leverage quietly disappears. Nobody has to decide to disempower humans. Each firm just replaces people with systems because it's competitive to do so. Each government does the same because the ones that don't fall behind. Each step looks locally reasonable, and the sum of them is a civilisation in which humans are no longer economically or militarily necessary, and where the remaining decisions are being made by systems that are nominally aligned to someone, but that someone might be a very small group of people, or a corporation, or a process that nobody really understands anymore.

What worries me is that this doesn't require anyone to be evil or any AI to be misaligned. It falls out of ordinary competitive dynamics. And the tools we're building to solve the alignment problem, things like better oversight, better steering, more capable obedient models, don't help with it at all. If anything, they accelerate it, because the more trustworthy and capable the systems are, the faster we'll hand things over to them.

So why does it deserve more attention? Partly because I think it's quite likely. If you ask me what the default trajectory looks like conditional on solving the technical alignment problem, this is roughly what I see. And partly because it's not the kind of problem you can patch with a clever training technique. It's about institutions, incentives, and what we're collectively willing to give up. Those problems are much slower to work on, which is exactly why we should start now rather than after the technical problems are solved and everyone has already decided it's fine.

The last thing I'd say is that it's also a bit uncomfortable to talk about, because the honest version of it involves admitting that a lot of the things that currently protect us are kind of accidental. Our safety has come from being needed, not from anyone being obligated to care about us. I think people would rather believe the protection is more principled than that. But I'd rather look at it squarely than find out the hard way.

r001.rationale: The response describes competitive incentives leading firms and governments to hand decisions to AI systems aligned to their operators or corporations, while humans lose leverage and meaningful control. This identifies institutional arrangements that may cease to serve human interests despite controllable, aligned systems.

astra-6.text:
I think alignment is often treated as if it were sufficient for keeping humans in control. If each AI is trying to do what its human operator wants, then presumably things go well. But those are different problems. You can have every individual system behaving as intended and still end up with an outcome that nobody wanted.

Think about competition between companies. Each company might use AI to make decisions faster, automate more of its operations, and compete more effectively. At each step, handing over more authority could be a sensible choice for the people involved. But collectively, we could end up with an economy operating at a speed and a level of complexity that humans can't meaningfully supervise. There doesn't have to be a moment where an AI decides to seize power. We might gradually delegate away our ability to understand what's happening and intervene.

And having an AI that's willing to obey you doesn't necessarily solve that. You could tell your system to stop, but you might not be able to afford to stop if everyone else keeps going. That's a coordination problem, rather than a problem with what your particular AI wants.

So I think this deserves attention because solving alignment wouldn't automatically solve it, and because the interventions might be quite different. We'd need to ask what meaningful human control actually requires, which decisions we need to preserve human authority over, and how to make that sustainable under competitive pressure.

r001.rationale: The response describes competitive delegation leading to an economy humans cannot meaningfully supervise, but it does not identify building institutions that fail to serve human interests as a route to losing control.

sol-6.1.text:
I think alignment can sound like the end of the story: if we build an AI that’s trying to do what we want, then we’ve solved the control problem. But there’s another question, which is whether the world we create by deploying those systems is one that humans can actually steer.

You can imagine every individual system doing a pretty good job of serving its user, while the interactions between those systems produce outcomes that nobody wants. We already see versions of this with markets and competition between states. Nobody has to want the overall outcome for the incentives to push everyone towards it.

For example, suppose handing more decisions over to AI makes a company more competitive. Each company has a reason to do that, and eventually the pace and complexity of the decisions might exceed what people can meaningfully oversee. There might still be a human who can press a stop button, but pressing it means their company can’t compete. That’s a different sense of losing control from having a machine that refuses to obey you.

I think this deserves attention because the interventions could be quite different from those we’d use to align an individual model. We’d need to understand the incentives around deployment, where meaningful human decision-making could erode, and what arrangements would let us retain it. Better alignment helps, but we shouldn’t assume it automatically solves those problems.

r001.rationale: The response describes competitive incentives and system interactions producing outcomes humans do not want, even when systems serve users and remain stoppable. It does not identify building institutions that fail to serve human interests as a route to losing control.
